Incorporating the Financial Stability Report, the assessment tilts more negative than the initial read. The FSR indicates the U.S. entered the shock with elevated vulnerabilities—stretched valuations, high nonfinancial business leverage, and material funding risks in prime money market and other open‑end funds—while the March 2020 turmoil exposed fragilities even in core markets (Treasuries, dollar funding). These amplify downside risks to activity and credit supply beyond the growth hit implied by the COVID demand/supply shock alone. That said, the report also notes banks’ strong capital/liquidity and that swift policy actions—rate cut to the ELB, large‑scale Treasury and agency MBS purchases, expanded repos, lower IOER/discount rate, and dollar swap lines—helped restore market functioning and reduce tail risks, supporting the transmission via lower term premia and eased funding strains. Net: near‑term outlook remains clearly negative with elevated financial stability risks, but decisive interventions materially mitigate the severity and duration of the downturn.
